storyboard.claim: Sitting back and waiting for the employee to set the agenda looks passive to a new manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card; the word PASSIVE carries the worry.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the new manager from the previous beat, now stuck in the one-on-one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the objection the chapter will answer.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, leaning back in her chair with a relaxed, uncertain look while the colleague talks.

storyboard.claim: A manager who waits for her report to steer the meeting seems to have lost control.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager leaning back at her desk while her colleague does the talking across from her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the new-manager worry as a visible scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the appearance of weakness the narration describes.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, leaning forward across a table and listening closely to someone out of frame.

storyboard.claim: The strongest move in a one-on-one is listening, not dominating.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Campbell leaning forward at a table, fully attentive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the worry: passivity is reframed as control.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Campbell as the model for the listening coach.

storyboard.claim: Campbell's colleagues called it free form listening, and listening is power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the technique from the previous line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the technique its name, free form listening.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, calmly watching the colleague who is thinking hard and drawing a plan on a notepad.

storyboard.claim: Letting the employee set the agenda lets the manager evaluate how they think.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manager quietly observing a colleague who is working out a plan on paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the silence reveals.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the evaluation as an observed behaviour, not a metaphor.

storyboard.claim: Coaching how to think and prioritize beats handing over a to-do list.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text list with three short steps set against the phrase TO-DO LIST.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts the coaching approach with simply assigning tasks.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the three things the employee learns to do.

image.subject: An engineer's desk with two monitors and a code editor open, a manager standing beside it with her hands in her pockets, not touching the keyboard.

storyboard.claim: The one-on-one is not for fixing code or copy, it is for developing the person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager beside an engineer's workstation, hands off the keyboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ties the previous point to the core thesis of the book.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the point concrete with a workstation.

image.subject: A young engineer in a casual sweater standing alone at a glass-walled office whiteboard, drawing a plan with confidence while a manager sits back in a chair across the room watching.

storyboard.claim: The goal is an employee who operates autonomously within the wider team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The engineer working out a plan alone at the whiteboard while the manager watches.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the workstation point to autonomy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows autonomy as the engineer working without being told what to do.

image.subject: A glass-walled boardroom with a long conference table, six people seated around it in animated discussion, a whiteboard with diagrams behind them.

storyboard.claim: A business moves forward through collective decisions and group dynamics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Six people in a boardroom debating around a long table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from one-on-ones to the group meeting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the group setting for the rest of the chapter.

image.subject: A group of a dozen office workers in business clothes walking together into a glass-walled meeting room, folders and laptops in hand, the door held open by one of them.

storyboard.claim: Strong individuals must be gathered into one room to decide the company's future.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A dozen colleagues walking into the same meeting room together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the coached individuals into one room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size and mix of a leadership group.

storyboard.claim: What happens when the group is deadlocked on a critical issue?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: What happens when they are deadlocked?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from group dynamics to a specific tense case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the Google conference room scene.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, measured and attentive, seated at the head of a long conference table in a Google conference room, two empty chairs in front of him.

storyboard.claim: The scene takes place in Eric Schmidt's conference room at Google, under visible tension.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Eric Schmidt at the head of a long conference table with empty chairs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the question to the scene location.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places Schmidt as the CEO managing the dispute.

image.subject: Two men in their forties in dark suits sitting at opposite ends of a long conference table, arms folded, both looking away from each other.

storyboard.claim: A bitter turf war has broken out between two senior executives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives at opposite ends of a table, arms folded, refusing to look at each other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the dispute set up in the scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hostility as body language.

image.subject: A smartphone lying face up on a conference table, with two sets of hands reaching for it from opposite sides.

storyboard.claim: The two executives are fighting over who owns a massive new mobile app.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A phone on a table with two pairs of hands reaching for it from opposite sides.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the prize in the turf war.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the object at the centre of the dispute.

left.label: EXECUTIVE A
left.subject: A senior executive in a dark suit, jaw set, leaning toward the table with his finger raised to make a point.

right.label: EXECUTIVE B
right.subject: A senior executive in a dark suit, arms crossed, shaking his head and not moving forward in his chair.

storyboard.claim: Two big egos are colliding in the dispute.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives in opposition, one leaning in and one refusing to yield.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the two sides of the feud.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the two egos side by side.

image.subject: Two men in suits walking side by side down a glass-walled office corridor toward a small meeting room, one carrying a laptop, the room door already open.

storyboard.claim: Schmidt sends the two feuding executives off to gather data and return with a compromise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two executives walking together toward a small room to work it out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows Schmidt's diplomatic move.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the rule Schmidt uses.

image.subject: A conference table with two laptops facing opposite ways, each screen showing a different chart, and no one reaching across to the other side.

storyboard.claim: The rule of two fails because both executives protect their own teams.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two laptops turned away from each other on a table, each showing a rival chart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows why the compromise approach is failing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the entrenched positions visible.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, the posture of a football coach, sitting at the edge of a conference table and quietly watching a heated argument.

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell sits in the room, watching the debate turn personal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell at the table's edge, silent and watching the argument.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings Campbell into the scene as the turning point.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows Campbell still and observant before he speaks.

storyboard.claim: Campbell cuts through the diplomacy and orders the two executives to break the tie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quote card with the line set large.
storyboard.onScreenText: Either you two break that tie or I will cut the...
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Campbell speaks after the silent watching shown in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the exact line Campbell uses to force the decision.

storyboard.claim: That moment defines the manager's role in decision making.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes Campbell's ultimatum with the one-word verdict.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the lesson of the scene in one word.

storyboard.claim: Leaders are taught that getting everyone to agree is the mark of good leadership.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: Isn't getting everyone to agree the hallmark of leadership?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the common belief the book challenges.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the conventional view to be overturned.

image.subject: A manager at the head of a round conference table with five colleagues, each one speaking in turn, the manager sitting with open hands and listening.

storyboard.claim: You want an ensemble that feels heard, but the job is not to find consensus.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A round table of colleagues speaking in turn while the manager listens with open hands.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the agreement question with a nuance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the ensemble approach as the right way to gather ideas.

image.subject: A whiteboard in a glass office with a lukewarm compromise written on it in faded marker, a half-erased line and the marker set down on the tray.

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell hated consensus because it produces watered-down compromises.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard with a faded, compromised plan on it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why consensus is rejected.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the idea of a watered-down result physical.

left.label: OFFENDS THE FEWEST
left.subject: A cautious committee of five people nodding politely around a conference table, nobody pushing an idea.

right.label: OPTIMAL
right.subject: A single bold sketch on a whiteboard drawn by one engineer, bright and specific, with the marker still in hand.

storyboard.claim: Deciding to offend the fewest people rarely produces the best decision.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A polite committee on the left, one bold sketch on the right.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the cost of consensus.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts the safe decision with the innovative one.

image.subject: A manager at a glass whiteboard with a numbered checklist of steps, marker in hand, reviewing the steps with two colleagues seated nearby.

storyboard.claim: The manager's job is to run a rigorous process.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager at a whiteboard working through numbered steps with colleagues.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the critique of consensus into the manager's real task.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the process as a visible checklist.

storyboard.claim: A rigorous process surfaces all dissent, lets the team debate, then the manager breaks the tie if needed.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text list of three steps.
storyboard.onScreenText: SURFACE DISSENT / DEBATE FIERCELY / BREAK THE TIE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the steps of the process the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the sequence the manager follows.

image.subject: A manager at the head of a conference table pointing decisively at one of two printed proposals, nodding with a firm expression, the other proposal pushed aside.

storyboard.claim: When the team cannot align on the data, the manager breaks the tie without hesitation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pointing to one proposal and pushing the other aside.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the final step of the process.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the decision as a physical act at the table.

storyboard.claim: How do you get every dissenting idea on the table before breaking the tie?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: How do you get the dissent on the table first?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks for the specific mechanical rule behind the process.
storyboard.addedInformation: Leads into the Marissa Meyer example.

image.subject: A young woman executive in her thirties in a tailored blazer, seated at the head of a conference table with her hands folded, listening quietly.

storyboard.claim: Campbell gave a rising executive a strict, non-negotiable rule for running her team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A young woman executive at the head of the table, hands folded, silent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the example behind the mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the rule into a specific leader's meeting.

storyboard.claim: What was the rule Campbell gave her?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the answer the next beat reveals.
storyboard.addedInformation: Builds suspense before the rule is named.

storyboard.claim: The leader always speaks last.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the rule in its shortest form.

image.subject: A young woman executive in a blazer at a conference table, mouth closed, holding a pen loosely, while colleagues around her speak and gesture.

storyboard.claim: Blurting out the answer at the start shuts down the conversation, even when the leader is right.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The leader holding back while others speak.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the rule matters for a brilliant leader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows restraint from a leader who already knows the answer.

image.subject: A small team of four around a whiteboard, each adding a line to the same diagram, the marker passing from hand to hand.

storyboard.claim: Speaking last lets the team reach the answer together.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Four team members taking turns at a whiteboard diagram.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the benefit of the rule in a team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the collaborative process visible.

image.subject: A young team member holding a printed proposal and making a point with one raised finger, colleagues around the table nodding and taking notes.

storyboard.claim: The team exercises decision making by debating, analyzing and arguing its points.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team member arguing with a proposal while colleagues take notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes what the team does when it is given room.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the argument as a healthy exchange.

image.subject: A row of silent team members sitting with their hands folded, all turned toward an empty chair at the head of a long table.

storyboard.claim: Without the rule, teams sit passively waiting for the leader to speak.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Team members looking at an empty chair at the head of the table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the failure the rule prevents.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the passive team physically visible.

storyboard.claim: In a fast-paced environment, speed is everything, so why should the leader hold back?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Raises the objection to speaking last.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the crisis example.

image.subject: An engineer at a desk late at night with two monitors showing a red error log, a colleague leaning over her shoulder to look at the screen.

storyboard.claim: A critical bug crashing the servers seems to justify skipping the debate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two engineers at night looking at a red error log on monitors.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the strongest version of the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the urgent case in a real engineering setting.

image.subject: A stopwatch resting on a desk beside a printed chart of falling revenue, the chart's edge pressed under a coffee mug.

storyboard.claim: Debating the best solution for an hour seems to waste precious time and revenue.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A stopwatch and a falling revenue chart on a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the cost of the delay.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cost of time as objects on the desk.

image.subject: A manager at a desk with a wall calendar, calmly circling a single date while a colleague looks on, the desk otherwise tidy.

storyboard.claim: Most daily tasks are not emergencies, so the false assumption is the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A calm manager circling one date on a wall calendar.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the objection by naming the false assumption.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the difference between an emergency and a normal day.

image.subject: A Silicon Valley office building at night with one floor lit and an orange emergency glow on the glass, an empty street below.

storyboard.claim: A real crisis, with servers down and a PR disaster unfolding, is a literal emergency.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A quiet office building at night with one floor lit by an emergency glow.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concedes the objection a genuine emergency exists.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the distinction the next line draws.
